title: The Five Great Vows of Jainism: IB Paper 1 Guide
summary: Five great vows in Jainism explained for IB World Religions SL, with key terms, sect differences, primary texts, themes, and Paper 1 revision.
body_markdown:
The five great vows of Jainism are **ahiṃsā** (non-violence), **satya** (truthfulness), **asteya** (non-stealing), **brahmacarya** (chastity or disciplined sexuality), and **aparigraha** (non-possession or non-attachment). Together, they provide an ethical path through which Jains seek to stop new karma from binding to the soul and remove accumulated karma.


That direct answer matters for IB World Religions SL. But a strong Paper 1 response must go further. The vows connect ethics to Jain teachings about the soul, karma, rebirth, liberation, ascetic practice, and community.


Jainism appears in Part 1 rather than as an in-depth study option. Your task is breadth with precision: define the vows, explain why they matter, recognize differences between monastic and lay practice, and connect them to the prescribed framework. The[RevisionDojo introduction to Jainism](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-19-jainism-an-introduction/notes) provides useful context before you revise each vow.


### The five vows at a glance


Sanskrit term Core meaning Monastic ideal Lay application


Ahiṃsā Non-violence Avoid injury in thought, word, and action Minimize harm through diet, work, consumption, and conduct


Satya Truthfulness Speak only what is true and non-harmful Avoid lies, deception, and damaging speech


Asteya Non-stealing Take nothing not freely given Reject theft, fraud, exploitation, and unfair acquisition


Brahmacarya Chastity Complete celibacy Practise fidelity, restraint, and responsible conduct


Aparigraha Non-possession Renounce property and attachment Limit possessions and resist greed or excessive attachment


A useful revision checklist is simple:


- Learn each Sanskrit term and an accurate definition.
- Explain its relationship to **karma** and **mokṣa** .
- Distinguish the **mahāvratas** from the **aṇuvratas** .
- Include Śvetāmbara and Digambara perspectives where relevant.
- Connect ethics to texts, practices, and religious experience.
- Apply the vows to the three fundamental questions.


### Why the vows matter in Jainism


The word **vrata** means a vow or solemn religious commitment. Ascetics follow the five as **mahāvratas** , or “great vows.” Lay Jains observe limited forms called **aṇuvratas** . A householder cannot usually avoid property, employment, travel, or family relationships, so the discipline is adapted to life in society.


This distinction reflects a central Jain idea: actions affect the condition of the soul. A soul, or **jīva** , is naturally conscious and capable of liberation, yet becomes entangled with karmic matter through actions and passions. Students can review this framework in RevisionDojo’s notes on[jīva, ajīva, and the weight of karma](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-192-the-human-condition-jiva-ajiva-and-the-weight-of-karma/notes) .


Observing the vows supports **saṃvara** , the stopping of new karmic influx. Ascetic discipline also contributes to **nirjarā** , the shedding of existing karma. The destination is **mokṣa** , liberation from **saṃsāra** , the cycle of death and rebirth. The vows therefore answer more than “How should a Jain behave?” They address how a soul can become free.


### Understanding each of the five great vows


### Ahiṃsā: non-violence


**Ahiṃsā** is the commitment not to injure living beings. It is often regarded as the organizing principle of Jain ethics because every living being possesses a soul. Harm can occur through action, speech, intention, negligence, or encouraging another person to act violently.


The Ācārāṅga Sūtra, an important text in the Śvetāmbara canon, presents restraint toward living creatures as fundamental to ascetic life. This helps explain vegetarianism, careful movement, filtering water in traditional contexts, and occupations chosen to reduce harm. Practices vary, so students should not reduce Jainism to its most visible ascetic examples.


Ahiṃsā also shapes the other vows. A factually truthful statement may still be wrong if it is spoken to cause avoidable injury.


### Satya: truthfulness


**Satya** requires truth in thought, speech, and conduct. It prohibits lying, deliberate misrepresentation, malicious accusations, and deception that harms others.


Its relationship with ahiṃsā creates an important interpretive point. Truthfulness prohibits falsehood, but truthful speech should also be careful and non-harmful. This shows that the vows form an interconnected discipline rather than five isolated commands.


### Asteya: non-stealing


**Asteya** , also called **acaurya** , means not taking what has not been given. It includes theft but can extend to fraud, dishonest measurement, exploitation, or improper use of another person’s property.


An ascetic accepts only what is freely offered under appropriate conditions. For a householder, the vow guides commerce, employment, ownership, and responsible consumption. This wider meaning gives asteya contemporary relevance without suggesting that all Jains reach identical conclusions.


### Brahmacarya: chastity


For monks and nuns, **brahmacarya** means celibacy and the renunciation of sexual activity. For householders following an aṇuvrata, it generally means sexual restraint, fidelity, and control of desire.


Defining brahmacarya only as celibacy ignores lay Jain life, while defining it only as moderation understates the monastic vow. In both settings, its purpose is mastery over passions that strengthen attachment.


### Aparigraha: non-possession and non-attachment


**Aparigraha** is the renunciation of possessions and possessiveness. Jain ascetics pursue radical non-possession, although its visible expression differs between communities. Laypeople usually place limits on acquisition and cultivate detachment from property, status, relationships, and preferences.


The vow concerns more than owning fewer objects. A person can possess little while remaining consumed by envy. Aparigraha addresses both external accumulation and the internal habit of building identity around possessions.


Two students discuss non-attachment while one guards an enormous pile of pens


### Mahāvratas and aṇuvratas


The Tattvārtha Sūtra, traditionally associated with Umāsvāti or Umāsvāmi, identifies the five vows and distinguishes complete from partial observance. It is especially useful because it is respected across the principal Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions, although textual versions and interpretations differ.


The **mahāvratas** involve comprehensive renunciation by ascetics. The **aṇuvratas** allow householders to move in the same spiritual direction while maintaining family and social responsibilities. Ascetics treat complete restraint as the clearest route to stopping karmic bondage. Householders use limited vows, generosity, worship, and support for ascetics as meaningful stages of spiritual progress.


These are not separate moral systems. They are related forms of discipline within the fourfold Jain community of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.


### Śvetāmbara and Digambara perspectives


The two major branches are **Śvetāmbara** , meaning “white-clad,” and **Digambara** , commonly translated as “sky-clad.” Both affirm the five vows, karma, rebirth, liberation, and the authority of the Jinas or Tīrthaṅkaras. Differences concern scripture, ascetic clothing, monastic discipline, and the spiritual status of women.


Śvetāmbara monks wear white robes, while Digambara monks ideally renounce clothing as an expression of complete non-possession. Digambara nuns wear robes. Digambara tradition has historically taught that final liberation requires rebirth as a man, whereas Śvetāmbara traditions accept that women can attain liberation directly. Aparigraha is therefore a useful example of how a shared vow can be interpreted through distinct ideals of ascetic perfection.


Avoid presenting either branch as more authentically Jain. Establish shared foundations first, then explain differences precisely. RevisionDojo’s overview of[Mahāvīra and the Jain community](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-191-jainism-in-context-mahavira-and-the-jain-community/notes) provides further context.


### The three fundamental questions


The vows become easier to remember when organized around the IB framework.


### What is the human condition?


The soul is caught in saṃsāra because karma binds it to embodied existence. Violence, dishonesty, theft, uncontrolled desire, and attachment intensify this bondage. Human life is valuable because disciplined understanding and conduct make spiritual progress possible.


### Where are we going?


The goal is mokṣa. A liberated soul escapes rebirth and manifests its intrinsic qualities without karmic obstruction. This is not salvation granted by a creator deity. Jain teachings emphasize purification through knowledge, faith, and conduct.


### How do we get there?


The path is expressed through the **Three Jewels** , or **ratnatraya** : right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. The five vows belong especially to right conduct, but practice also depends on understanding and spiritual orientation. They connect Jain doctrine with the pursuit of liberation.


### Connecting the vows to the five themes


For IB World Religions Jainism revision, do not file the vows under ethics and stop there.


- **Rituals:** Confession, repentance, fasting, almsgiving, and monastic practices reinforce restraint and purification.
- **Sacred texts:** The Ācārāṅga Sūtra describes ascetic non-violence, while Tattvārtha Sūtra 7 discusses vows and their forms.
- **Doctrines and beliefs:** The vows depend on teachings about jīva, karma, saṃsāra, saṃvara, nirjarā, and mokṣa.
- **Religious experience:** Fasting, meditation, renunciation, and disciplined awareness can transform how practitioners experience desire and other living beings.
- **Ethics and moral conduct:** The vows govern intentions, speech, consumption, relationships, occupations, and possessions.


This approach matters because Paper 1 prompts may require you to connect a concept with evidence rather than recite a definition. The[RevisionDojo guide to studying religion](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-11-the-study-of-religion/notes) helps distinguish description, interpretation, and evaluation.


### A Paper 1 response method


Begin with the term. Define it accurately, connect it to Jain doctrine, and give one relevant expression of practice. Then add nuance through the monastic and lay distinction or a Śvetāmbara and Digambara comparison.


For example, an answer about aparigraha could define non-possession or non-attachment, explain that attachment attracts karma, contrast ascetic renunciation with lay limits on property, and connect the vow to mokṣa. That sequence turns memorized vocabulary into religious understanding.


Use the[IB World Religions resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) to combine Study Notes and Flashcards for recall with Questionbank practice for application. RevisionDojo’s[World Religions misconceptions guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) and[mock exam preparation plan](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-mock-exam-prep-november) can help you test whether your explanations remain precise under timed conditions.


### From five words to one coherent path


The five vows are easy to list. Their significance is harder to understand. Each limits conduct that binds the soul, while together they turn Jain beliefs about life, karma, and liberation into a disciplined way of living.
